comment: Hesiod addenda: Theogony catalogues and Works and Days calendar (Evelyn-White 1914).

region.zh: 大地、海洋與星空（神話地理）

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 411-452

summary.en: Asteria, daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, bore Hecate, whom Zeus honoured above all: a portion of earth, of the barren sea, and of starry heaven; and whoever calls on her in prayer is heard, for she stands by kings in assembly, by horsemen in battle, by athletes in contest, by fishermen at their nets, and with Hermes increases the herds in the pens. She is nurse of all children who see the light of Eos; and her honours, given in the beginning, are never taken away.
summary.zh: 科俄斯與福柏之女阿斯特瑞亞生赫卡忒，宙斯予其榮光超越諸神：大地一份、荒海一份、星空一份。凡祈禱者皆蒙垂聽：她伴君王於議會、騎士於疆場、健兒於賽場、漁夫於網前；又與赫爾墨斯共掌畜群之興衰；並為初見晨光之孩童的乳母。其榮光自始不受剝奪。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Phoebe came to the bed of Coeus, and the goddess, pregnant with the god's love, bore dark-robed Leto, ever gentle, kind to men and to the deathless gods — kindest of those on Olympus. Phoebe also bore honourable Asteria, whom Perses led to his great house to become his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 404-410 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Asteria bore Hecate, whom Zeus, Cronos' son, honoured above all others. He gave her splendid gifts: a portion of the earth and the barren sea, a share of the honour from the starry skies, and the highest honours from the immortal gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 411-416 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now, whenever humans on the earth pray for favours by offering beautiful sacrifices, they call on Hecate: much honour follows the ones whose prayers the goddess kindly accepts, and fortune follows those so blessed — such is her power. For all those born to Gaia and Ouranos were granted honours, and Hecate had her share too. Nor did the son of Cronos seek to deprive her of any honour she received from the Titans, and she retains all she was given in the beginning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 416-422 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: When men arm themselves for deadly combat, she stands beside her chosen side, eager to grant victory and extend glory; she stands beside revered kings in the courts of justice; she stands beside horsemen, and beside those competing in the games. To those who work the gusty grey sea and pray to Hecate and the roaring Earth-shaker, she grants a great haul of fish, and just as easily takes it away. And along with Hermes she excels at increasing livestock in the pens, and can strengthen a herd or a flock or weaken it, whatever her spirit desires. And though she is her mother's only child, she is granted great honours among the immortals; and Cronos' son made her nurse to all children who see with their eyes the light of all-seeing Eos.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 422-452 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Nereus and the Fifty Daughters of Doris
title.zh: 涅柔斯與多里斯的五十女兒

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 233-264

summary.en: Pontus fathered the truthful Nereus — the Old Man of the Sea, gentle and kind, who never forgets what is due and makes fair and honest plans — and Nereus, wedding Doris, daughter of Ocean, had fifty daughters in the barren sea. Of them all, the poet names only a handful before going through the rest: Protho, Eucrante, Sao, Amphitrite, Eudora, Thetis, Galene, Glauce, Cymothoe, Speo, Thalia, Pasithea, Erato, Eunice, Melite, Eulimene, Agave, Doto, Proto, Pherusa, Dynamene, Nessea, Actaea, Protomedea, Doris, Panope, Galatea, Hippothoe, Hipponoe, Cymodoce, Cymatolege, Cymo, Eione, Halimede, Glauconome, Pontoporea, Leagore, Euagore, Laomeda, Polynoe, Autonoe, Lusianassa, Euarne, Psamathe, Menippe, Neso, Eupompe, Themisto, Pronoe, Nemertes.
summary.zh: 旁托斯生下「海上老人」涅柔斯——溫厚誠實、不忘道義、謀劃公正；涅柔斯娶大洋之女多里斯，於荒海中生下五十位女兒：普羅托、歐克拉忒、薩奧、安菲特里忒、歐多拉、忒提斯、伽勒涅、格勞刻、庫墨托厄、斯佩俄、塔利亞、帕西忒亞、厄拉托、歐尼刻、墨利忒、厄利墨涅、阿伽瑪、多托、普洛托、費魯莎、狄娜墨涅、涅賽亞、阿克泰亞、普洛托墨狄亞、多里斯、帕諾珀、伽拉忒亞、希波托厄、希波諾厄、庫墨多刻、庫墨托勒革、庫摩、厄俄涅、哈利墨得、格勞科諾墨、蓬托波瑞亞、勒阿戈瑞、歐阿戈瑞、拉俄墨達、波呂諾厄、奧托諾厄、路西安那薩、歐阿耳涅、普薩瑪忒、墨尼珀、涅索、歐篷珀、忒彌斯托、普羅諾厄、涅墨耳忒斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Pontus fathered truthful and sincere Nereus, his eldest child: they call him the Old Man, for he is gentle and kind, never forgets what is due, and makes fair and honest plans.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 233-236 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he mixed again with Gaia and begat great Thaumas, arrogant Phorcys, fair-cheeked Ceto, and Eurybia, whose heart is of steel. And many children, all greatly desired, were born in the barren sea to Nereus and fair-haired Doris, daughter of ever-circling Ocean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 237-242 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: These came from the illustrious Nereus: fifty daughters, all able to do great work — from Protho and Eucrante to Psamathe and Menippe, Neso and Eupompe, Themisto, Pronoe and Nemertes — sea-maidens whose company fills the waters of the Greek world, and of whom Thetis and Amphitrite would one day wed heroes and gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 240-264 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 337-370

summary.en: Tethys bore to Oceanus the river-gods of the world — Nilus, Alpheus, Eridanus, Strymon, Meander, Ister, Phasis, Rhesus, the silver-eddying Achelous, Nessus, Rhodius, Haliacmon, Heptaporus, Grenicus, Aesepus, divine Simois, Peneius, Hermus, Caicus, the great Sangarius, Ladon, Parthenius, Euenus, Aldescus, and divine Scamander — and with them the daughters who with lord Apollo and the Rivers raise up young boys to be men. And there are three thousand more rivers, says the poet, too many for a mortal to name, but each known to the people who live beside it.
summary.zh: 忒堤斯為俄刻阿諾斯生下世間諸河神：尼羅河、阿爾甫斯、厄里達諾斯、斯特呂蒙、邁安德、伊斯特爾、法西斯、瑞索斯、銀旋的阿克洛俄斯、涅索斯、羅狄俄斯、哈利阿科門、赫普塔波魯斯、格瑞尼科斯、埃塞波斯、神聖的西摩伊斯、珀紐斯、赫爾穆斯、開科斯、大桑伽里烏斯、拉冬、帕爾忒尼俄斯、厄維諾斯、阿爾得索斯與神聖的斯卡曼德羅斯；此外還有三千條河，凡人無法一一唱名，卻皆為鄉人熟知。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Tethys bore to Oceanus the twisting rivers: Nilus, Alpheus, the deep-swirling Eridanus, Strymon, Meander, beautiful Ister, Phasis, Rhesus, the silver-eddying Achelous, Nessus, Rhodius, Haliacmon, Heptaporus, Grenicus, Aesepus, divine Simoeis, Peneius, Hermus, fair-flowing Caicus, the great Sangarius, Ladon, Parthenius, Euenus, Aldescus, and the divine Scamander.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 337-355 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And she bore divine daughters who raised young boys into men, along with lord Apollo and the River-gods — for so Zeus charged them: Peitho, Admete, Ianthe, Electra, Doris, Prymno, divine-formed Ourania, Hippo, Clymene, Rhodea, Callirrhoe, Zeuxo, Clytie, Idyia, Pasithoe, Plexaura, Galaxaura, welcoming Dione, Melobosis, Thoe, shapely Polydora, fair-formed Cerceis, doe-eyed Pluto, Perseis, Ianeira, Acaste, Xanthe, charming Petraea, Menestho, Europa, Metis, Eurynome, saffron-veiled Telesto, Chryseis, Asia, fair Calypso, Eudora, Tyche, Amphiro, Ocyrhoe and Styx, who is without doubt the greatest of them all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 355-362 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: These were the oldest of the maidens born to Oceanus and Tethys; but there are many others: three thousand thin-ankled daughters of Oceanus spread across the earth and the watery depths, all equal, shining children of goddesses. And many other loud-flowing rivers, sons of Oceanus, were born to queen Tethys; their names are difficult for a mortal to recite, but each is known to those who dwell beside them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 362-370 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: The Farmer's and the Sailor's Year

region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（赫西俄德故鄉，象徵性定位）

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 383-694

summary.en: Hesiod sets out the working year by the stars: the Pleiades, Hyades, Orion, Sirius and Arcturus mark ploughing, harvest, threshing and sailing. Plough when the Pleiades rise and fall; harvest when Orion and Sirius are in the sky; cut wood when the leaves have fallen; thresh when Orion rises; sail fifty days after the solstice, when the sea is smooth, and bring the ship up on the sixth after the grape-picking is done. The story is the mythic origin of the Greek agricultural calendar: the stars are the gods' own clock, and the labourer who misses a season goes begging to his neighbours.
summary.zh: 赫西俄德以星辰劃分勞作之年：昴星團、畢宿、獵戶座、天狼星與大角星各標耕作、收穫、揚場與航行之時。昴星升落則犁地；獵戶與天狼當空則收割；葉落則伐木；獵戶升起則揚場；夏至後五十日宜航行；摘葡萄後第六日當收船。此即希臘農事曆之神話起源：星辰乃神明之鐘，誤時之勞作者唯向鄰人乞食。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod tells Perses to observe the signs from Zeus. The Pleiades, the Hyades, the strength of Orion, and the Bear, which men also call the Wagon, wheel about in the same place, and watch Orion: they alone bathe in the stream of Ocean. It is by the Bear that sailors steer, for she is bright and beautiful to see.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 383-397 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Harvest the crops when Pleiades, Atlas' daughters, begin to rise, and plough when they are about to set: for forty nights and days they are hidden, and again, as the year moves round, they first appear when the iron is being sharpened. This is the law of the plains and the sea-coast, and of the fertile glens far from the troubled deep: sow naked, plough naked, and reap naked, if you will harvest Demeter's work in due season.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 415-426 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Orion and Sirius come into mid-sky, and Arcturus rises in rosy-fingered Dawn, then, Perses, cut your grapes, and bring them home; expose them to the sun ten days and ten, then five in the shade, and on the sixth draw the cups of the joyous wine-gift of Dionysus. And when Orion and Sirius come mid-sky, and Arcturus sees the rosy-fingered Dawn, then Perses, cut your grapes — that was the sign for the whole of the Greek vintage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 609-617, 656-668 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: For sailing, fifty days after the solstice is the season, when toilsome summer is come to its end: then there is no wind to break a ship, and no man to drown; unless Poseidon the Earth-shaker or Zeus wills it, for they are the keepers of the ends of the sea. But the wind is trustworthy then, and the sea, and the sea is tranquil: put the freight on board, and make for home quickly, and do not wait for the new wine and the autumn rain and the winter's harm, for the sea is then dangerous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 663-678 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.
